entities.summary:
Milan Cathedral (Duomo di Milano) is the largest Gothic cathedral in Italy and the third largest in the world, built primarily from 1386 to 1965 — a construction period of nearly 600 years. Dedicated to the Nativity of Mary, it sits at the physical and symbolic heart of Milan, and its extraordinary marble façade, 135 spires, and 3,400 statues make it one of the most complex Gothic structures ever built.

Construction began under Gian Galeazzo Visconti, Duke of Milan, in 1386, with the Duke promising to fund the whole project — which he did not. For centuries, the common Milanese expression 'fabbrica del Duomo' ('cathedral workshop') meant a project that would never be completed, because construction so often halted when funding ran dry. Napoleon Bonaparte ordered the façade completed in 1805 for his coronation as King of Italy in the cathedral.

The Duomo's roof terrace is a unique architectural feature, accessible since medieval times, allowing visitors to walk among the forest of marble spires and statues. The golden Madonnina statue (4.16 meters tall) on the highest spire (108.5 meters) has been Milan's guardian since 1774; a Milanese law historically prohibited any building from exceeding her height — a rule gradually relaxed as modern skyscrapers rose. The Last Supper by Leonardo da Vinci, painted nearby at Santa Maria delle Grazie, was created during the same era as the Duomo's nave construction.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Milan Cathedral's nearly 600-year construction history, extraordinary sculptural program, and role in Napoleon's coronation make it both a Gothic masterpiece and a monument to Italian civic and religious identity.
